DUI checkpoints, random stops, etc, I've found that as long as you are nice, look them in the eye, do exactly what they say, and look as least threatening/suspicious as possible they'll not bother with taking it any farther.

Old buddy of mine is a cop. We used to hang out back in the day and have a lot of mutual friends.

I had a headlight out, it was 2AM and raining. In the mirror I see the cherries and berries flashing. I pull over.

I see who it is, he see's it's me. We stood there and caught up for about fifteen minutes. He told me to get my headlight fixed. I said I would.

I drove home.

That's the only time I've been pulled over.

"Have you had anything to drink?"

"Not yet!"

Officer proceeds to laugh so hard he had to lean on my car for a minute.

"Okay, I'd better not catch you going the other direction then."

If you respect the individual in direct encounters, you get respected in kind. I've been let off a bunch of times, im not putting it down to "smooth talking" but definitely not being a dick to someone is gonna help you find yourself on the side of discretion. Its just common sense.

When I was younger my sister and I helped our dad get out of a ticket. He was speeding on a highway, and the cop pulled him over. Both my sister and I weren't feeling well so he tries to pull that "I am trying to get to somewhere my kids can throw up". Cop wasn't believing him at first and my sister and I only gave him five minutes before we opened our car doors and threw up. He let us get going.

If you get pulled over on the highway wait until the cop gets up to your window and asks for your info. Once he does, lean your head out the window and look at the road. Look up at the cop and say "Am I pulled over far enough that you're not in danger? I can pull over a little farther if you need me to." The cop will think you are responsible and not an asshole.

Doesn't always work, but it's gotten me out of a couple.
Is college worth it? Is this even the right question?

This article takes an interesting though not very uncommon perspective. Basically, they say college graduate success rates are down because students are less dedicated to school. They paint this false picture that American students are lazy and undedicated, itself a lazy conclusion. The fact remains that students entering college in the US are unprepared because primary school there are terrible. For example, in the US you do algebra, over and over, until you graduate from high school. If you happen to be in the subset of kids that show particular math aptitude, you might get a chance to an elementary calculus or statistics class, but only if your school happens to offer it. Similar trends can be shown in formal writing, reading complex literature, etc.

Also, the last part of article focuses on this asinine notion that this is somehow linked to young people not reading newspapers. Well, 1999 just tweeted, it wants its zeitgeist back. I'm frankly surprised newspapers even exist anymore in countries where people have easy access to the Internet on their ubiquitous mobile phones.
